Let's sketch the situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068082/assets/e283660466c42f7723d9e044bb2eefe148c468f7dae5a1b5882e2589e7e5f60a.png)

Note the following:

- The dotted line is the *perpendicular bisector* of the segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$

- All the points on this perpendicular bisector are equidistant to $A$ and $B.$

- Our task is to find the point $Q$ on this line that's closest to $P.$

First, we create a function $S$ which represents the *squared* distance between the point $P(4,5)$ and a general point $Q(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-5)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-5)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8x-10y+41\end{aligned}
$$

The required point $Q(x,y)$ is equidistant to the points $A(-7,2)$ and $B(3,2).$ So, by writing down $(QA)^{2}=(QB)^{2},$ we have the following constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{(x+7)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{(QA)^{2}} & ={{(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{(QB)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

We make $x$ the subject in the constraint equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+7)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+14x+49+(y-2)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-6x+9+(y-2)^{2} \\ \cancel{{x}^{2}}+\cancel{(y-2)^{2}}+14x+49 & =\cancel{{x}^{2}}-6x+9+\cancel{(y-2)^{2}} \\ 14x+6x & =9-49 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our expression for $S(x,y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =(-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}-8(-2)-10y+41 \\  & =4+{y}^{2}+16-10y+41 \\  & ={y}^{2}-10y+61.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the first derivative,

$$
{S}^{′}(y)=2y-10,
$$

and solve ${S}^{′}(y)=0$ to find the stationary point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 2y-10 & =0 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Let's verify that this stationary point is a minimum. Taking the second derivative, we find

$$
{S}^{″}(5)=2>0.
$$

We conclude that the stationary point $y=5$ indeed minimizes the squared distance. 

Therefore, the required point is $(\,-2,5\,).$
